tables.title: Cross-model transaction
tables.dataset: Vector hit to graph traversal to document update, in one transaction
conditions: The engines do not all run the same SHAPE of filtered search, and it shows in the recall column as much as the time one. ArangoDB, MongoDB, Neo4j (vector index), PostgreSQL + pgvector + AGE, Qdrant + Neo4j (no shared transaction), SurrealDB (embedded), and SurrealDB (server) restrict the candidate set first and rank what is left by distance, so they return that set's true nearest matches. ArcadeDB (one transaction) and ArcadeDB (server, one transaction) instead take an over-large global top-k and keep whichever candidates happen to fall inside it: more work, and a partial answer, because a global list of that size usually does not contain enough of the candidates. Read both columns for those arms as what this query shape costs rather than as what the engine can do.

The transaction is the update, and every engine here commits it all or nothing. ArcadeDB (one transaction), ArcadeDB (server, one transaction), Neo4j (vector index), and PostgreSQL + pgvector + AGE also run the vector search and the hop inside it; ArangoDB, MongoDB, SurrealDB (embedded), and SurrealDB (server) run those two reads first and wrap only the update (MongoDB cannot do otherwise: it refuses a vector search inside a multi-document transaction, and its rows record the refusal). One client runs at a time, so the answers are the same either way. Qdrant + Neo4j (no shared transaction) has no transaction spanning its two systems, which is what that row exists to show.
Disk is what the workload left on disk, in GiB: the engine's writable layer plus its volumes after the cell, minus the same engine's empty footprint.

ArangoDB's row is marked `re-run`: its rows on this table were measured before the index on the product id that the protocol builds for it existed, so its reads scanned every product. They are withheld until it is measured with the index.

SurrealDB's graph-filtered search is marked `re-run`: our query scanned every product instead of reading the candidates by record id, the access path every other engine on this table was given. It is being re-measured with the fix.

SurrealDB (server) retrieval at the 500k tier is marked `re-run`: the server was still building its vector index in the background when these queries ran. It is being re-measured with the build waiting for the index to catch up.

Qdrant + Neo4j's row is marked `re-run`. Its vector half ran in the Qdrant client's in-memory local mode, a pure-Python reimplementation rather than the Qdrant server, so every time, recall, and disk value it produced described that reimplementation. It is being re-run against the Qdrant server the vector table uses. Its all-or-nothing result on the atomicity table below does not depend on this.

Neo4j's row is marked `re-run`: its vector index ran at Neo4j's default quantization, binary with a three-fold search expansion, which our index definition did not override, so its vector search was not the unquantized search the other engines ran. The next measurement sets the quantization explicitly. Its all-or-nothing result on the atomicity table does not depend on the index.

SurrealDB (server)'s transaction cells are marked `re-run`: the server ran at its default, a sync to disk at every commit, although it has a setting that does not wait, and every other engine on this table that has such a setting ran at it. Our harness missed that setting, and the next measurement runs the transaction at it.
There is no cold column on this table, and the reason is recorded on the rows themselves: no cold/warm split: each operation runs against an already-built, already-warm database by construction

Durability is matched at the relaxed end: on every engine that has the setting, a commit returns without waiting for the disk and the log is flushed by the engine's own background policy, which is ArcadeDB's engine default and a documented production mode for each of the others. Each row records what it ran as `durability`, and the setting was read out of the engine rather than assumed on every engine except ArcadeDB (server, one transaction) and SurrealDB (server). ArcadeDB (server, one transaction) is given the setting when the server starts, and the row records it, because the server offers no way to read it back. SurrealDB (server)'s rows record that no setting was found, and its server log shows what it ran: its default in both runs, a sync to disk at every commit (the log reads "Sync mode: every transaction commit" in every run), although it has a setting that does not wait; the next measurement runs both. ArcadeDB (one transaction) loaded its catalog with the write-ahead log off, which the bulk-load helper it used does by default, so its ingest figures had less durability than the relaxed setting; its timed operations ran with the log on. The next measurement loads with the log on.

Atomic means all or nothing: the whole update happens, or none of it does, with no state in between that anyone can observe. One engine can promise that across a vector, a graph edge, and a document because they share a transaction. Qdrant and Neo4j cannot promise it to each other, because nothing spans the two.

So the interesting result here is not the speed. It is what a crash halfway through leaves behind, and the atomicity table below shows it: for each engine, how many interrupted writes left the store holding some but not all of the write after it was reopened. That is what this comparison exists to show.

tables.title: Session cost, open to close
conditions: The SESSION is open + action + close. Reporting open and close alone hides work triggered between them.

Cold start is measured in a fresh subprocess and reported beside every session number, because a millisecond open inside a process that takes half a second to reach its first database call is not a millisecond to whoever launched it.
A clean close should be O(what was written), not O(what is stored): write nothing and closing should cost the same at 10k documents and 10M.

Server rows have no JVM start, first open, or cold process: the server is already running when the probe connects, so those three columns describe the embedded process only. The session columns are measured for both.
Graph with the analytical view is withheld: its query grew from a bounded set of seeds to an unbounded 2-hop, so it stays off this table until the next measurement bounds the query again.

SurrealDB's peak memory on this table is withheld, and its 10M dense-vector cell is not shown: our build fed SurrealDB from one in-memory Python list while the ArcadeDB arm streamed, so its memory reading was partly ours, and the 10M vector build was killed for our allocation, not SurrealDB's. Its session timings ran after the build and stand. Both are re-measured in the next measurement, with the input streamed.
An engine with no row for a situation cannot build it, and its adapter says so rather than leaving the row blank; the declared row keeps the statement the adapter tried and the engine's own answer.
SurrealDB (embedded) has no row for the graph with the analytical view (no graph analytical view) or sparse vectors (no sparse-vector index type).

The dense-vector rows' one-query and write-then-query sessions, embedded and server alike, carry a defect in the engine build measured here, ArcadeDB issue #8852 (https://github.com/ArcadeData/arcadedb/issues/8852): the first vector search after a database is reopened re-reads every vector's record on one thread, so from a million vectors up those sessions are mostly that re-read, and ArcadeDB 26.10.1 fixes it.

The rows each session reads back are hashed, and for documents, documents with ten indexes, the graph, and time series every embedded engine that builds the situation must return the same hash as ArcadeDB embedded, or nothing is published. Only ArcadeDB (embedded) builds sparse vectors, so there is no second answer to compare. Not compared: the empty database, which reads nothing back; and dense vectors, whose read goes through an approximate index and is checked by recall on the dense vector table instead. The server rows are compared only with other server rows, because a server session runs a different set of modes and its record counts differ by construction; ArcadeDB (server) is the only engine served here, so they are compared with nothing.

ArcadeDB's embedded dense-vector rows read the index's statistics just before close, to record whether a rebuild ran. The read is outside the timers, but on this engine build it raises the cost of the close that follows it, so that row's open and close figure is an upper bound for a session that touches nothing.

SurrealDB rows have no JVM start: the SurrealDB core is a compiled extension that the Python import loads, so there is no runtime to start apart from the import. Their first open is the first open with the SDK already imported, and their cold process is interpreter start, import, open, and close, the same span the ArcadeDB embedded rows time. SurrealDB's time-series row is a plain table of timestamped records, the footing its time-series rows elsewhere on this page run on, because the engine has no time-series type.

SurrealDB (embedded) at 10M: the cell for documents with ten indexes reached the 28g memory envelope (peak 28,672 MiB) and was killed by the kernel, the same envelope every engine on this table had; it did not run out of time, and there is no row.

SurrealDB (embedded) at 10M: the cell for the graph reached the 28g memory envelope (peak 28,672 MiB) and was killed by the kernel, the same envelope every engine on this table had; it did not run out of time, and there is no row.
